stories.headline: Update: Iran Sets Conditions for Talks With US, Says 'Not a Gram' of Enriched Uranium Will Leave Country
stories.summary:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, said Tuesday that Tehran will not surrender any enriched uranium and will not negotiate with the United States until Washington takes steps to rebuild trust. Rezaei made the remarks after meeting in Pakistan with army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and repeated them in a post on X.

"Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran," Rezaei wrote. He added that "there will be no negotiations until the United States takes steps to build trust," and said the process must begin with the "full fulfillment of all Iran's conditions." Iranian officials have framed those conditions as including the lifting of sanctions and an end to U.S. threats.

The statement sets out Tehran's public position as the Middle East war continues to widen, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi and Yemeni targets and the Trump administration trading warnings with Iran. President Trump has accused Iran of killing Americans and protesters, and Vice President Vance has said the U.S. has "decisively won" the war "in some ways." Iranian officials have said they also have "unfinished jobs" should the U.S. renew attacks.

Pakistan's role as host of Tuesday's meeting suggests it is acting as an intermediary, and Qatar is preparing a regional defense agreement. The dispute over Iran's enriched uranium stockpile remains the central obstacle to any negotiated settlement, and the two sides' stated preconditions leave little visible room for talks in the near term.

stories.headline: Musk Says Tesla-SpaceX Merger Under Active Consideration
stories.summary:
Elon Musk said Tuesday that a merger of Tesla and SpaceX is under active consideration. Speaking on a call with analysts after SpaceX's quarterly results, he said, "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes." He said special committees at both companies have been formed to examine the idea but have not reached agreement on terms and that there is no guarantee they will.

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at about $2 trillion, a combination would be one of the largest mergers in history. At least 50% of Tesla shareholders would need to approve it, a threshold Musk called "quite a high hurdle." He said he is not on either committee and described himself as a "conflicted party" as CEO of both firms, likening even discussing the topic to "tap dancing through a minefield."

SpaceX shares rose 8% in after-hours trading and Tesla shares gained 2%. SpaceX's quarterly results showed $7.5 billion in revenue from its cloud compute business, which serves customers such as Anthropic and Google, and $5.2 billion from Starlink. The company remains unprofitable, with $1.1 billion in losses so far this year.

Musk has been consolidating his businesses; SpaceX acquired xAI and X before going public earlier this year, and Tesla and SpaceX recently launched the joint Terafab chip manufacturing effort. Musk said a full merger would make sense given overlapping work in chips, AI and software. Tesla reports its own quarterly results Wednesday.

stories.headline: Trump Sued Over 50% Tariffs on Canadian Goods
stories.summary:
The Liberty Justice Center, the group that successfully sued over President Trump's "liberation day" tariffs, filed a new lawsuit in the U.S. Court of International Trade challenging the latest levies on Canadian goods. The suit was brought on behalf of Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey food business that pays 50% tariffs on imported Canadian cheese. It asks the court to find the tariffs unlawful and order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The White House imposed the 50% levy on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, ranging from wine and dairy to hockey sticks, after trade talks between the two countries broke down in August. The administration relied on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which targets foreign discrimination against U.S. commerce. Trump cited what he called "unequal treatment" of American cars, dairy and alcohol. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by matching the U.S. tariffs "dollar for dollar."

The plaintiffs argue Section 338 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and that even if it applies, the administration has not established a legal basis. They also say the law requires a 30-day waiting period, yet the cheese tariff was added to the list just a week before collection began. Liberty Justice Center chief executive Sara Albrecht said the case concerns the presidency, not Trump personally: "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf."

The White House has been contacted for comment. The administration has generally defended its tariff authority as necessary to counter unfair trade practices, while business groups say the costs ripple through supply chains.

stories.headline: Nigeria Confirms Ebola Case in Abuja in Woman Who Arrived From Uganda
stories.summary:
Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive, the Health Ministry said. She developed symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital on Oct. 11, where she was diagnosed. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities are tracing 44 contacts.

Uganda's Ministry of Health said the patient, a Nigerian woman on a business trip to eastern Congo, only transited through Uganda and that exposure there is not established. It insisted Uganda has no confirmed active cases. Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality or when she arrived.

Nigeria is the latest country to report a case in the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain, which began in Congo in mid-May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has recorded nine infections since. Africa CDC director general Jean Kaseya said the outbreak is "the most geographically extensive in history," spanning several countries across three regions, with a fatality rate near 50%.

Nigeria set up an Ebola task force in June and stepped up surveillance two weeks ago. Chief of staff Femi Gbajabiamila said at the time the government did not want a repeat of a past outbreak when a carrier entered the country and officials scrambled to respond.

stories.headline: Ohio Governor's Race Turns Ugly Over Viral Video Featuring Acton's Estranged Mother
stories.summary:
A viral 60-second video targeting Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton is roiling the Ohio governor's race, where she faces Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy. The clip features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter "a liar" and urging Ohioans to vote against her. It remains unclear who produced the spot.

Acton's campaign condemned the ad and alleged that Ramaswamy's campaign is behind it. Her brother called it a "despicable low" and said the family's stepfather sexually abused Acton when she was a child. Meghan McCain, daughter of the late Sen. John McCain, a Republican, also criticized it on X, calling it "dastardly" and saying it never should have been created. She added, "Shame on whatever consultant firm created this."

The controversy comes as the race tightens in its final two weeks. NBC News reporting describes the contest between Acton and Ramaswamy as having become very close. Coverage of the ad's origin and the campaigns' responses is continuing, and the dispute is likely to shape the closing stretch of one of the Midwest's most closely watched midterm contests.

stories.headline: Fact Check: How the US Economy Is Performing Under Trump Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
As the midterm elections approach, President Donald Trump has been touting the economy, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. He has repeatedly said, "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world." BBC Verify examined whether the evidence supports those claims.

The overall economy is growing at a respectable pace, with GDP expanding at an annualized 2.2% and up about 3.2% since the end of 2024, more than any other G7 member over that period. Growth has outpaced International Monetary Fund forecasts made after the April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs, partly because Trump eased the tariffs in the following months. An AI investment boom has also helped, with monthly data center construction spending of $5 billion in August 2026, almost double the rate when Trump returned to office.

Inflation is a weaker point. The current rate is 3.7%, well below the 9% peak in 2022 under President Joe Biden but above the 3% Trump inherited in January 2025. Economists estimate inflation would be lower without the tariffs, and the US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted energy supplies and pushed up fuel prices, including diesel. The analysis also warns the economy could falter if AI spending dries up.

stories.headline: Update: Suspect Arrested in Limoges Town Hall Fire as French Cities Extend Curfews
stories.summary:
French media report that a 34-year-old suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested over the fire that gutted the 19th-century city hall in Limoges on Saturday. The clock tower and parts of the roof collapsed during the weekend's mass disorder. The man is known to police for violence against public officials and is on a national security watchlist, according to FranceInfo and BFM TV.

Authorities are also widening curfews. Marseille will impose an overnight curfew on minors in commercial areas from Tuesday to Friday, Paris is extending its overnight curfew for as long as necessary, and Lyon renewed its curfew. Nice and Lille curfews continue, and Bordeaux began a week-long curfew. Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 149 people were in detention and asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament a large police presence would meet demonstrators at a protest planned for Saturday, and accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan. Jean-Luc Melenchon of La France Insoumise demanded he "prove his accusation" or apologize, while urging followers to show restraint. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who admitted police had "lost control" in some cities, offered to resign Monday, but President Emmanuel Macron rejected it. The protests were over fuel prices, the cost of living and declining public services.

stories.headline: Update: Man Charged in Attack on Australian MP Helen Haines to Appear in Court
stories.summary:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after independent MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in Victoria on Monday. He is due in court Wednesday on charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. Local media named him as environmental activist Brendan Nugent.

Haines, 65, who holds the seat of Indi, remains in critical but stable condition after surgery in Melbourne and is reported to have lost a leg. Police say they will allege the incident was targeted, but that it appears isolated with no other known threats. Nugent's father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines for more than 20 years and called it a "shocking and horrific crime."

A local barber, Ricky Jefferies, said he pulled the suspect from the car. Police said a highway patrol unit was on scene within eight seconds of the call. Vigils were held in Wangaratta, where bouquets are gathering outside her office, as the country reacts with shock amid reports that threats to Australian politicians had been rising.

stories.headline: Sudan Army Drone Strikes Reportedly Kill More Than 300 at Funeral Convoy and Fuel Market
stories.summary:
Drone strikes attributed to Sudan's army have reportedly killed more than 300 people in two areas of West Kordofan state and the disputed Abyei region, according to sources cited by the BBC. The Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict, said 150 people died in strikes on Sunday evening, including a truck carrying about 200 mourners that was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab. A further 150 people were injured in those attacks, and a market in Al-Mujlad was also bombed, with casualty figures there not yet known.

On Monday, a drone strike on a market in Abyei killed 153 people, the region's information minister said. A military source told the BBC the army carried out the Abyei attack, describing the market as a fuel supply site for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The army has not responded directly to the allegation over the other strikes but has said it does not attack civilians, even when it believes RSF fighters are among them.

The Abyei attack has raised tensions between Sudan and South Sudan, which jointly administer the oil-rich area and both claim ownership of it. South Sudan summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest, and there are fears the fighting could spill across the border.

The war between the army and the RSF, which erupted in 2023, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the organization is alarmed by continued deadly drone strikes, noting that 20 million people face acute hunger and that famine risk is rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Armed drones are increasingly the weapon of choice despite a partial arms embargo.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Strikes Kill Two Girls in Besieged Yemeni City of Taiz as UN Warns of 'Grave Risk'
stories.summary:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a residential area in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, on Tuesday, killing two teenage girls and wounding six people. UN human rights chief Volker Turk said the Houthis have largely encircled the city, cutting off most supply routes and placing civilians at grave risk. The UN says the siege has left many residents without food and other necessities as prices soar.

The attack followed a Houthi strike a day earlier on a government military camp that killed 73 recruits, which a senior Yemeni government official called the deadliest strike since the conflict resurged over the summer. Fighting escalated after government and Saudi-led coalition forces launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire. Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February, and the Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognized government.

Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis on Tuesday, though the kingdom has struggled to defend against the group's missile and drone attacks despite its U.S.-supplied arms. Britain announced it would expand military support for Saudi Arabia to include defensive air patrols by Royal Air Force jets.

Turk urged that humanitarian aid be allowed into Taiz immediately and that civilians wishing to leave be allowed to do so safely. He also called on both the Houthis and government forces to avoid using explosive weapons in populated areas. Yemeni government forces claimed they thwarted Houthi attacks in several areas, a claim the Associated Press could not verify.

stories.headline: CDC Recognizes Third U.S. Measles Death as 2026 Cases Pass 4,400
stories.summary:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has added a third U.S. measles death to its national tracker, with total cases for 2026 now surpassing 4,400. The Department of Health and Human Services told Reuters the CDC updated its count after the National Center for Health Statistics received a report of a measles-related death.

The federal count still falls short of the number recorded by Pennsylvania, according to the report, indicating a discrepancy between state and national tallies. The new death was added to the federal tally as the country continues to record one of its largest measles outbreaks in decades.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that can cause severe complications, particularly in young children and unvaccinated people. Health officials have repeatedly stressed vaccination as the primary means of preventing its spread.

stories.headline: Update: Albertans Vote Decisively to Remain in Canada, Carney Says
stories.summary:
Albertans voted by an overwhelming majority to remain part of Canada in Monday's referendum, according to preliminary results. Final ballots were still being counted, but the remain side's lead was described as decisive. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans had made a "clear choice" to stay in the country.

The vote followed days of coverage about whether the province would begin a legal path toward a separation referendum. The result is a major setback for Alberta's separatist movement. Analysts quoted in coverage said separatists might now try to challenge Premier Danielle Smith's leadership.

Independence was not the only question on the ballot. Albertans also voted on measures including the introduction of voter ID and restrictions on immigration, and those results were being watched closely as counting continued.

The outcome removes, for now, a significant threat to national unity in Canada. Attention turns to how the final tallies on the other ballot questions play out and how the separatist camp responds to its defeat. Coverage came from outlets across the spectrum, including BBC News, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, NPR, Al Jazeera and the New York Times.

stories.headline: Update: Curfews Bring Calm to Paris as France Cracks Down on Rioters
stories.summary:
Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend of the most destructive rioting France has seen in years. Authorities imposed localized curfews in several cities to prevent a new round of looting. In the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter monitored Place de la République overnight.

At least 2,400 people were arrested after Saturday's clashes, which occurred during nationwide protests over rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. According to the Justice Ministry, roughly 2,500 people have been arrested since Saturday, and more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday noon. About 300 people in Paris alone were referred to prosecutors.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the targeted curfews helped keep the night calm and that new ones would be imposed wherever the situation requires, decided by prefects and mayors. Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence deemed too lenient and promised the justice system would be "extremely firm."

The unrest continues to draw political debate. Fox News reported that activists are calling new protests, billed as "Acte II," for Saturday, Oct. 24, with 212 mobilizations planned, and said its investigation identified 101 left-wing groups across nine countries amplifying the protests. Critics on the left have focused instead on the economic grievances and school conditions that drove the demonstrations.

stories.headline: Republicans See Shrinking Boost From Mid-Decade Redistricting
stories.summary:
House Republicans are quietly scaling back expectations for the roughly 10-seat gain they sought from redistricting nationwide, according to Axios. The shift reflects a souring political climate and polls showing a collapse in GOP support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida.

Top GOP strategists told Axios that on their down days, Republicans privately worry the redistricting war of 2026 will net them only one seat nationwide. At the start of the cycle, the party viewed redistricting as an umbrella strategy to protect its House majority.

The effort has drawn criticism from Democrats and voting-rights advocates, who argue the new maps shifted Black voters into districts designed to create safe Republican seats. Republicans have defended the redraws as a legitimate use of state legislative authority. The reassessment comes as other coverage points to President Trump's weak approval ratings and Democratic strength heading into the midterms.

The analysis suggests the maps may deliver far less than intended if the national environment keeps favoring Democrats, with the midterm elections now two weeks away.

stories.headline: China Defends DeepSeek After US Government Ban, Warns of Retaliation
stories.summary:
China is pushing back against a Department of Homeland Security order to remove products from the Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from government systems, warning of potential retaliation. The order, dated July, was published in the Federal Register on Monday.

DHS said DeepSeek's AI models present "multiple threat vectors" and that use of the tools may result in the transfer of sensitive data to China. The ban covers DeepSeek products and tools built on DeepSeek by third parties, which must be removed from agency IT devices.

The move comes as the United States and China compete for dominance in artificial intelligence. Beijing has criticized the action as unjustified, while U.S. officials cite data security and national security concerns.

It remains to be seen what form any Chinese retaliation might take, and whether other countries or agencies adopt similar restrictions.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Accuses Iran of Killing Americans and Protesters as Qatar Prepares Regional Defense Agreement
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump sharply criticized Iran's government during remarks in Kansas on Monday. He accused the regime of killing Americans with roadside bombs and of hanging protesters from cranes. Fox News live coverage also reported that Qatar is preparing to announce a regional defense agreement, and that Iran has issued a warning to the United States.

Trump said Tehran had sought assurances about its own treatment. "They wanted me to guarantee that we won't kill them like we killed the others," he said, adding that Iran had "killed a lot of Americans with their roadside bombs over the years." He referred to the 2020 U.S. drone strike that killed Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani during his first term. He also claimed that Iranian authorities had killed at least 75,000 protesters in the last eight months, a figure that was stated in his remarks and was not independently verified in the reporting provided.

The remarks come as the Middle East conflict continues to draw in regional actors and as Washington debates how the war should end. Vice President JD Vance has said the U.S. has "decisively won" the war in some ways, while Trump has tied Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election to the question of whether the U.S. must "finish the job" against Iran. Critics of the administration question the strategy and the lack of a clear endpoint, while supporters say a hard line is needed to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

The Qatar defense agreement, if announced, would add a new element to the regional security picture. Further details of the pact and any Iranian response are expected in coming days.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky and US Envoys to Hold Oslo Talks as Rubio Denies Withholding Intelligence
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff are due to meet in Oslo, Norway, as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorate. Jared Kushner is to take part by video link. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Zelensky asked Norway and Finland to organize the meeting with the U.S. and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine." Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met Zelensky ahead of the talks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India, called accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the U.S. was withholding intelligence "scandalous" and "outrageous." The claims came from Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, who told the BBC that unreliable U.S. warnings were costing lives. Rubio acknowledged that Patriot interceptor missiles may not yet have arrived in Ukraine but said nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. Zelensky said he had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about early warnings, interceptors and Starlink service.

Tensions have grown in recent weeks. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president and for "somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Last week a bipartisan group of senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to Starlink in Ukraine. Trump also recently announced, after a call with Vladimir Putin, that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel and that U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports would end, a move that drew criticism including from some Republicans.

Store said the aim of the talks is to steer relations toward "a more constructive path" and a lasting, just peace. It is unclear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia, though Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hopes a meeting can be organized soon.

stories.headline: Update: Marseille Braces for More Unrest After Weekend of Looting and Violence
stories.summary:
Marseille is preparing for further unrest after Saturday's protests turned into widespread disorder in France's second city. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, most of them looted, including shops along La Canebiere, Rue Paradis and the Centre Bourse shopping centre, as well as malls in the city's north.

A police union official described the weekend as "apocalyptic." Arnaud Blaise of the UN1TE union said, "It was a war," calling the violence unprecedented. In Marseille, 118 officers were injured, more than a tenth of the national total, and 101 arrests have been made, a quarter of them children. Blaise attributed the chaos to far-left agitators and said young people from deprived northern suburbs exploited it to steal; this characterization is his own and was not independently established.

On Monday authorities banned demonstrations and gatherings for eight hours, and the city was largely calm, with police far more visible than protesters. An overnight curfew for minors will take effect in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. A suspect has also been arrested after the historic town hall in Limoges was set alight, according to French media.

Some demonstrators defended the protests' aims while condemning the looting. One 18-year-old student described the march's solidarity as "beautiful" and the later disorder as "terrifying." The government faces mounting political pressure after the nationwide riots, in which about 1,800 people were arrested.

stories.headline: Michigan Senate Race Enters Final Two Weeks as Rogers Targets El-Sayed's Support Among Black and Jewish Voters
stories.summary:
Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers said at a Fox News town hall Monday night that Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is vulnerable among two traditionally Democratic blocs, Black and Jewish voters. The Michigan contest is one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Election Day on Nov. 3.

Rogers said Black pastors and neighborhood leaders in Detroit are "looking for a change," and pointed to El-Sayed's past remark that Barack Obama was "not the right choice" to advance a progressive agenda. Obama is scheduled to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Oct. 24 and has released a video backing him. Rogers also said that if half of Michigan's roughly 70,000 Jewish Democrats voted for him, it would bring about 35,000 votes and change the race's dynamic.

Rogers cited El-Sayed's criticism of Israel. In a recent debate, El-Sayed declined to say whether he considers Iran or Israel the greater threat, saying both "have proven dangerous in their own way." Republican gubernatorial nominee John James and Rep. Lisa McClain also appeared, seeking to tie Michigan Democrats to government spending and the party's progressive wing.

El-Sayed's campaign and Democrats have argued that he represents a new generation focused on affordability and working-class concerns, and Obama's involvement is intended to consolidate the party's base. The race is part of a broader midterm landscape in which President Trump's approval has fallen to record lows, giving Democrats an edge in some polling.

stories.headline: Albanian Protesters Clash With Police for Seventh Day in Bid to Oust Prime Minister Rama
stories.summary:
Protesters in Albania fought with riot police on Monday for the seventh consecutive day. The demonstrators, many of them high school and university students, are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Their grievances include poor university conditions and anger over corruption. Official figures said 295 people had been injured before Monday's violence, 186 of them police officers.

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the unrest. Rama, brandishing a rock thrown at police on Sunday, told police chiefs that "the moment the state negotiates with this, the state has fallen." He said the protesters included young people "radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US" and claimed Albania had become the target of a "well co-ordinated attack."

A BBC correspondent in Tirana's Rinia Park watched protesters pry up cobblestones to use as projectiles. Police advanced with an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas, and riot squads chased the largely student crowd through the park. Human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani, who is providing legal support to more than 100 detainees, said police actions were often chaotic and that officers rarely present evidence in court. He said those who actually throw objects are seldom caught.

The movement has no formal leadership, and activists coordinate informally to arrange first aid, legal help and protest locations. Police, for their part, appear angered by the injuries to their colleagues. The standoff shows no sign of easing, and the government has so far rejected negotiation.

stories.headline: Japanese Spacecraft Launches Toward Mars' Moon Phobos to Retrieve Sample
stories.summary:
A Japanese-led spacecraft launched Tuesday on a mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons, where it will attempt to collect surface material and return it to Earth. If successful, it would be the first sample ever returned from Mars or its moons. The Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission is led by the Japanese space agency JAXA and is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

The spacecraft will first study the smaller moon Deimos as it approaches, then focus on Phobos, which is about 20 km across. It plans to deploy a small rover to scout a landing site, a difficult task because Phobos has very little gravity while sitting next to Mars' much stronger gravitational pull. The main craft will then touch down, use a robotic arm and two samplers to collect about 10 grams of dust, and send it back in a capsule landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia in 2031.

Scientists hope the sample will resolve how Mars' moons formed. One hypothesis holds that a space rock struck Mars early in its history and the moons formed from the debris. The other holds that they are asteroids from the outer Solar System captured by Mars' gravity. Sara Russell of the Natural History Museum said the two ideas would produce very distinct chemistry and mineral results, so the answer should be quickly apparent. Researchers say even a tiny sample can support extensive study of individual grains.

stories.headline: Rep. Garcia Says ICE Officers Broke U.S. Citizen's Arm in Long Beach
stories.summary:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers broke the arm of a U.S. citizen in North Long Beach over the weekend. "ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen. The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country," Garcia said.

Police in Long Beach said ICE called them for backup and that officers arriving at the scene found a man who was bleeding and handcuffed. The details of what led to the confrontation and the extent of the man's injuries were not fully laid out in the available reporting, and it was not clear whether DHS had responded to the allegation.

The episode adds to an ongoing national debate over immigration enforcement tactics. Democrats and immigrant advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized aggressive ICE operations and cited cases involving citizens. Supporters of the enforcement push, including the administration, generally argue that officers face resistance and that agents act within the law. Further information from DHS, Long Beach police and the man's representatives is expected.

stories.headline: Air Force Sergeant Dies After Fall During Pregame Ceremony at Alamodome
stories.summary:
A U.S. Air Force member died after falling while abseiling from the ceiling of San Antonio's Alamodome before a college football game on Saturday. Footage showed the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf at midfield during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy. The dome's ceiling is about 170 feet high.

The military identified him as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio and a member of the 57th Wing. He died in hospital. Patterson, of Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served 15 years and was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the headquarters level in 2022.

The incident is under investigation. The game went ahead as planned, and the American Conference said the decision to continue was made before his death was confirmed. Brig. Gen. Scott Mills said the tragedy was "felt deeply across the 57th Wing," and UTSA president Taylor Eighmy offered condolences to Patterson's family and fellow airmen.
